claims: El Niño is a climate pattern marked by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean.
El Niño causes weakened trade winds.
El Niño typically lasts 9–12 months.
El Niño appears every 3-5 years.
El Niño often brings wetter conditions to the US South.
El Niño often brings warmer winters to the North.
El Niño brings suppressed Atlantic hurricane activity.
El Niño brings wetter, cooler conditions from California through the South and Atlantic coast of the United States.
Northern U.S. and Canada typically experience warmer, drier winters during El Niño.
El Niño often brings heavy rainfall and flooding to the west coast of South America (Ecuador/Peru).
El Niño often brings drier conditions to the western Pacific, including parts of Australia and Indonesia.
El Niño causes reduction in upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water along the Pacific coast.
The reduction in upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water along the Pacific coast disrupts marine ecosystems and fishing industries.
El Niño tends to reduce the number of Atlantic hurricanes due to increased wind shear.
El Niño develops when trade winds weaken.
Weakened trade winds allow warm water to move eastward.
El Niño lasts about 9 to 12 months.
El Niño often peaks during the winter months.
NOAA monitors El Niño through sea surface temperature monitoring.
NIWA monitors El Niño through sea surface temperature monitoring.
Increased likelihood of El Niño development is often identified months in advance.
